story.headline: Israel votes in first post–Oct 7 election
story.summary: Israelis are voting today, Tuesday 27 October, in the first Knesset election since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, and morning turnout was the highest since 1981.
story.display_body: Israelis are voting today, Tuesday 27 October, in the first Knesset election since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, and morning turnout was the highest since 1981. By 08:00 GMT, three hours after polls opened, more than 1.2 million people had voted, a turnout of 16.68%, said Dean Livneh, director of the Central Elections Committee. That is the highest figure at that point of the day since the 17% of 1981. About seven million Israelis are eligible to elect the 120-seat Knesset (Israel's single-chamber parliament). The main contest is between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Yashar, the centrist party of former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, who served as a minister without portfolio in Netanyahu's government from October 2023 to June 2024; RFI describes the race as very close. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust, which he denies, and is the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over the Gaza war. Al Jazeera notes that the main opposition bloc also runs on a right-wing security platform, so a change of government would not necessarily mean a change of policy towards the Palestinians.
story.why: the vote decides whether Netanyahu's coalition with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties survives, and it will shape Israel's course in Gaza, the West Bank and the wider conflict with Iran.

story.headline: UN rights chief warns of Hebron ethnic cleansing
story.summary: UN human rights chief Volker Türk warned on Monday 26 October that Israel's operation in the West Bank city of Hebron raises "serious concerns of ethnic cleansing", after more than 3,000 Palestinians were evacuated from their homes since Friday 23 October.
story.display_body: UN human rights chief Volker Türk warned on Monday 26 October that Israel's operation in the West Bank city of Hebron raises "serious concerns of ethnic cleansing", after more than 3,000 Palestinians were evacuated from their homes since Friday 23 October. The operation began after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three at a checkpoint near Hebron on Friday; both gunmen were killed. Türk said the operation had demolished homes and businesses and confined many residents to their neighbourhoods, and that statements by senior Israeli officials showed the measures were "punitive in nature and designed to instil fear". "Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," he said, calling for the displaced to be allowed home and compensated. The UN humanitarian office OCHA says more than 2,000 settler attacks causing casualties or damage have been recorded in the West Bank since the start of 2026, more than in any previous year on record.
story.why: it is one of the UN's strongest warnings yet about the West Bank, issued on the eve of the Israeli election.

story.headline: 32 governments warn of famine in Sudan
story.summary: The United States, the European Union and 30 other countries warned on Monday 26 October of an "alarming deterioration" in Sudan's food security and a risk of famine in the coming months, as a drone strike on a market in Nyala killed 21 people the same day.
story.display_body: The United States, the European Union and 30 other countries warned on Monday 26 October of an "alarming deterioration" in Sudan's food security and a risk of famine in the coming months, as a drone strike on a market in Nyala killed 21 people the same day. The joint statement, released by the US State Department and signed by countries including the UK, France, Germany, Canada and Australia, called on the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to lift all obstacles to aid, including air access to Darfur, and warned that the number of children with severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000. In Nyala, the RSF stronghold in Darfur where the army regularly strikes, a hospital worker told AFP the attack also wounded 40 people; it was not clear how many of the victims were RSF fighters. The RSF, for its part, hit six power stations on Sunday, cutting electricity in four eastern states, and attacked a power station in Khartoum early on Tuesday. The new strike adds to the UN's count of at least 306 people killed by drone strikes in three weeks, published last week.
story.why: the war, now in its fourth year, is already the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis, and the strikes on power stations threaten hospitals and water supplies for millions.

story.headline: Climate pledges cut emissions just 6% by 2035
story.summary: A UN synthesis of national climate plans published on Tuesday 27 October projects that global greenhouse-gas emissions will be only about 6% below 2019 levels by 2035, against the roughly 60% cut that scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5°C.
story.display_body: A UN synthesis of national climate plans published on Tuesday 27 October projects that global greenhouse-gas emissions will be only about 6% below 2019 levels by 2035, against the roughly 60% cut that scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5°C. The report from UN Climate Change (the UNFCCC secretariat) covers the nationally determined contributions (NDCs, the climate pledges each country must file under the Paris Agreement) of 154 countries, submitted between January 2024 and August 2026 and covering 71% of global emissions. Even if countries also met their conditional targets, the cut would reach only 9%. Last year the UN projected about 10%, but it then had to model many missing pledges, and the US has since left the Paris Agreement for a second time. To keep warming below 2°C, the Paris fallback goal, emissions would have to fall 37% by 2035. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said the COP31 conference in Antalya, Turkey, which opens on Monday 9 November, "can help address some of the key gaps".
story.why: the gap between pledges and what is needed is wider than a year ago, and it sets the starting point for the COP31 negotiations.

story.headline: Saudi, Turkey, Pakistan open Tehran talks
story.summary: Saudi Arabia and the coalition it leads in Yemen said they intercepted three ballistic missiles and four drones fired by the Houthis on Tuesday 27 October, while Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials held talks in Tehran on Monday 26 October to try to calm the regional war.
story.display_body: Saudi Arabia and the coalition it leads in Yemen said they intercepted three ballistic missiles and four drones fired by the Houthis on Tuesday 27 October, while Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials held talks in Tehran on Monday 26 October to try to calm the regional war. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said the missiles were aimed at Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and caused no casualties. Saudi Arabia sent its defence minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, to Tehran, Pakistan its army chief Asim Munir and Turkey its intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin; in a joint statement carried by Iranian state media, the four countries agreed to continue the dialogue. Separately, according to SRF, senior Houthi official Mohammed Ali al-Houthi said Egypt's decision to give Saudi Arabia defensive military aid amounted to a declaration of war on Yemen. The Saudi–Houthi front reopened after the US–Israeli war on Iran began in February.
story.why: the Tehran meeting is the first joint attempt by Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad to open a channel with Iran, while the Houthi threat against Egypt could widen the Yemen front.

story.headline: Jordan strikes Syria after church attack
story.summary: Jordan said late on Monday 26 October that its air force struck "militant hideouts" in southern Syria linked to last week's attack on a church in Karak, in which nine people were killed and 40 injured.
story.display_body: Jordan said late on Monday 26 October that its air force struck "militant hideouts" in southern Syria linked to last week's attack on a church in Karak, in which nine people were killed and 40 injured. Jordan says the strikes were coordinated with Damascus, but Syria gave a different account and has opened an investigation; a Syrian health official told the state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed. Earlier on Monday, Jordanian forces arrested three wounded suspects after a dawn shootout in Karak governorate. King Abdullah II had ordered an "iron fist" response.

story.headline: Oleshky aid truce takes effect
story.summary: Russia and Ukraine began a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky at 03:00 local time on Tuesday 27 October, to let humanitarian aid reach the roughly 2,000 people still trapped there.
story.display_body: Russia and Ukraine began a local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky at 03:00 local time on Tuesday 27 October, to let humanitarian aid reach the roughly 2,000 people still trapped there. Russia's defence ministry said its forces had stopped shelling in the Kherson sector, and Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said Kyiv was honouring the agreement; whether fighting actually eased could not be independently verified. The truce, announced on Friday 23 October, was brokered by US first lady Melania Trump. Up to 50 of them are children, and the UN says residents face severe shortages of food and medicine.

story.headline: Bolsonaro's party accepts Lula win
story.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party recognised Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election on Monday 26 October, and Bolsonaro dropped his demand to annul the vote, though he still has not conceded.
story.display_body: Flávio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party recognised Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election on Monday 26 October, and Bolsonaro dropped his demand to annul the vote, though he still has not conceded. In a statement the party said it recognised "the result proclaimed by the Superior Electoral Court", while asking for "clarifications" about social benefits Lula approved during the campaign. Bolsonaro now says he will ask the courts to invalidate Lula's candidacy for "abuse of economic and political power". US President Donald Trump called the vote "another rigged election", without giving evidence; Brazil's electoral-court president had said on Sunday that the two-hour extension of voting, which both campaigns requested in different regions, did not affect the result.

story.headline: Cassis to reopen Swiss office in Pyongyang
story.summary: Foreign minister Ignazio Cassis will visit North Korea on Thursday 29 and Friday 30 October to formally reopen Switzerland's diplomatic office in Pyongyang, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday 26 October.
story.display_body: Foreign minister Ignazio Cassis will visit North Korea on Thursday 29 and Friday 30 October to formally reopen Switzerland's diplomatic office in Pyongyang, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday 26 October. The office has been operating since 19 October and reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing. Cassis will hold talks with North Korean officials on restarting bilateral consultations between the two foreign ministries, on security on the peninsula and on global geopolitics, and then go to Seoul on 30–31 October. Switzerland has sat on the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission on the inter-Korean demarcation line since 1953 and is one of the few Western countries that has held a political dialogue with Pyongyang since 2003. The department says the presence should allow direct dialogue "including on subjects of disagreement", but does not say whether human rights or sanctions will be raised.
story.why: it gives Switzerland one of the very few permanent Western diplomatic presences in North Korea, and a channel it can offer as a go-between.

story.headline: Ebola patient treated in Geneva
story.summary: The Federal Office of Public Health confirmed on Monday 26 October that a Swiss woman with Ebola is being treated at Geneva University Hospitals (HUG), and that her husband, a close contact, is in isolation at Zurich University Hospital.
story.display_body: The Federal Office of Public Health confirmed on Monday 26 October that a Swiss woman with Ebola is being treated at Geneva University Hospitals (HUG), and that her husband, a close contact, is in isolation at Zurich University Hospital. The couple were flown from Nigeria by air ambulance on Monday. The office says she is infected with the Bundibugyo strain, and that there is no danger to the public: the virus spreads only through close contact with a person who has symptoms. HUG and USZ have been Switzerland's two designated reference hospitals for such diseases since 2019. Interior minister Elisabeth Baume-Schneider thanked Nigeria's health minister and the WHO for the repatriation.

story.headline: Health-cost round table adds six measures
story.summary: Health-sector representatives agreed on Monday 26 October to six new measures to contain health costs from 2027, but for the first time put no figure on the savings.
story.display_body: Health-sector representatives agreed on Monday 26 October to six new measures to contain health costs from 2027, but for the first time put no figure on the savings. The round table, set up by health minister Elisabeth Baume-Schneider in November 2024, brings together the cantons, doctors (FMH), hospitals (H+), health insurers (prio.swiss), the pharmaceutical industry, patient groups and the Price Supervisor. The measures cover more outpatient care, relieving hospital emergency departments, care programmes for the chronically ill, more detail on invoices for medical devices, coordinated medication in nursing homes and more treatment at home. The office says they are "more systemic" than the twelve adopted in 2025, so no savings can be estimated yet. It also reports that one of last year's measures, the push for electronic billing, has stalled over new disagreements, so its expected savings will not materialise in the short or medium term, and that actual savings from the 2025 package cannot yet be measured.
story.why: health-insurance premiums are one of the biggest household costs in Switzerland, and the round table is the government's main voluntary tool for slowing them, yet so far it has not put a number on what it saves.

story.headline: Swiss home prices rise 1.7% in Q3
story.summary: Prices of owner-occupied homes in Switzerland rose 1.7% in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the second, and 4.4% year on year, the Federal Statistical Office reported on Tuesday 27 October.
story.display_body: Prices of owner-occupied homes in Switzerland rose 1.7% in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the second, and 4.4% year on year, the Federal Statistical Office reported on Tuesday 27 October. Single-family houses rose 2.1% and condominium flats 1.3% over the quarter. The steepest increase, 3.4%, was in urban municipalities of small agglomerations or outside agglomerations, and the smallest, 0.6%, in "intermediate" municipalities. The residential property price index reached 129.8 points (end of 2019 = 100), meaning prices are about 30% higher than before the pandemic.
story.why: with collective-agreement wages up only 0.5% this year, home ownership keeps moving further out of reach for buyers.

story.headline: Social assistance reached 267,300 in 2025
story.summary: About 267,300 people, or 2.9% of the population, received social assistance in 2025, according to the first results of the Federal Statistical Office's overhauled social-welfare statistics, published on Tuesday 27 October.
story.display_body: About 267,300 people, or 2.9% of the population, received social assistance in 2025, according to the first results of the Federal Statistical Office's overhauled social-welfare statistics, published on Tuesday 27 October. That is 4.5% more people than a year earlier, though the office warns that comparisons with earlier years should be made with caution because of the change in method. The new statistics replace an annual survey with monthly, largely automated processing of data from about 1,000 mostly municipal social services, which the office says makes cantons and communes more comparable. The rate was highest among children and teenagers (4.8%), and among divorced (4.2%) and single people (3.7%), compared with 1.4% among married people.
